groups.name: Local statistical
groups.text: A separate model is fitted to each series.

groups.name: Intermittent demand
groups.text: Methods for series with many zeros (spare parts, retail).

models.name: Naive
models.summary: Repeats the last observation unchanged over the horizon.
models.how: The forecast equals the last value of the series and is flat over the horizon. It has no parameters.
models.use: The simplest benchmark. Hard to beat on series that behave like a random walk.
models.caution: Ignores seasonality and trend.

models.name: Seasonal naive
models.summary: Carries the values of the previous season forward.
models.how: Forecast(T+h) = y(T+h−m); m is the integer part of the largest seasonal period (same as the msts frequency in R). Series for which other models fail also receive this method as a fallback forecast, and these are counted and reported.
models.use: A baseline for seasonal data; also the fallback forecast.
models.caution: Not meaningful if the series is shorter than one period. It also carries the noise forward unchanged.

models.name: Simple exponential smoothing (SES)
models.summary: Smooths the level component with exponential weights; gives a flat forecast.
models.how: The single smoothing parameter (alpha) is chosen by maximum likelihood (alpha in the range 0.0001–0.9999). There is no trend or seasonality; the forecast is constant over the horizon.
models.use: Series without trend or seasonality, or whose seasonality is handled separately; a quick baseline.
models.caution: Makes systematic errors if there is trend or seasonality.

models.name: ETS (exponential smoothing state space)
models.summary: An exponential smoothing family that selects the error, trend and seasonality form automatically with an information criterion.
models.how: All combinations of additive/multiplicative error, trend (possibly damped) and seasonality are fitted; the information criterion picks the best.
models.use: A strong general-purpose classical method; common for monthly, quarterly and weekly data.
models.caution: Seasonality is not used if the period exceeds 24 (same rule as R ets); it cannot capture seasonality in long daily/hourly periods. In that case consider dhr_arima, mstl or tbats.

models.name: Theta
models.summary: Combines simple exponential smoothing with a drift equal to half the slope of the series.
models.how: If seasonality is detected by an ACF test, a classical multiplicative decomposition is applied; then the SES forecast and a linear drift with half the slope are added.
models.use: The method that won the M3 competition; a fast and robust baseline for short series.
models.caution: Does not handle complex multi-seasonal structures.

models.name: Random walk with drift
models.summary: Extends the line from the first to the last observation into the future.
models.how: Forecast(T+h) = y(T) + h·(y(T) − y(1))/(T − 1); the same rule as R rwf(drift = TRUE). It has no parameters.
models.use: A standard benchmark for trended series.
models.caution: Only the first and last observations determine the slope, so an outlier at either end changes the whole forecast.

models.name: Naive2 (M4 benchmark)
models.summary: Seasonally adjusted naive forecast; the reference method of the M4 OWA measure.
models.how: If a 90% autocorrelation test (M4 benchmark code, at least 3 periods of data) finds seasonality, a classical multiplicative decomposition removes it; the last adjusted value is repeated and the seasonal indices are put back.
models.use: Needed to compute OWA; a seasonal benchmark that is less noisy than seasonal naive.
models.caution: The seasonality test uses R's default number of autocorrelation lags, so long periods (e.g. 365 in daily data) are treated as non-seasonal.

models.name: Comb S-H-D (M4 benchmark)
models.summary: Average of simple, Holt and damped Holt exponential smoothing on the seasonally adjusted series.
models.how: Seasonality is removed as in Naive2; SES, Holt (linear trend) and damped Holt forecasts are averaged and the seasonal indices are put back. Holt parameters are fitted by least squares within the R ets bounds.
models.use: The combination benchmark of the M3/M4 competitions; strong and hard to beat on yearly, quarterly and monthly data.
models.caution: Same model as R holt() (ets AAN / AAdN, least squares). On NN5 the mean SMAPE and MASE are within 0.4% of R; single series can differ slightly because R's optimiser sometimes stops at a worse fit (docs/VALIDATION.md 1d).

models.name: Dynamic optimised Theta (DOTM)
models.summary: A Theta model whose theta coefficient and parameters are optimised and updated over time.
models.how: State-space form of the Theta method with an optimised theta line; seasonality is removed first by classical decomposition when detected.
models.use: A strong benchmark in M4 for yearly/quarterly/monthly data; also a component of SCUM.
models.caution: For series containing zero/negative values, additive decomposition is used instead of multiplicative (a note is recorded).

models.name: SCUM (median of ETS, CES, ARIMA, DOTM)
models.summary: Point-wise median of four automatic statistical models.
models.how: ETS, CES, ARIMA and DOTM are fitted with this engine's settings and the median of their forecasts is taken at each horizon step. If a component fails the median of the remaining ones is used (a note is recorded); with fewer than two the series falls back.
models.use: A simple combination that ranked among the best statistical benchmarks in M4; useful to test whether combinations change rankings.
models.caution: As slow as its slowest component (ARIMA); measure with a short trial first.

models.name: Combination: mean of ETS, ARIMA, Theta
models.summary: Equal-weight average of the automatic ETS, ARIMA and Theta forecasts.
models.how: ETS, ARIMA and Theta are fitted with this engine's settings and their forecasts are averaged at each horizon step. If a component fails the mean of the other two is used (a note is recorded); with fewer than two the series falls back.
models.use: The classic simple combination: it is often more accurate than each of its parts (Makridakis & Hibon 2000; Hyndman's ETS-ARIMA-Theta average was a strong M4 benchmark). Good for testing whether combining changes rankings.
models.caution: As slow as its slowest component (ARIMA). One badly wrong component pulls the mean; the median variant is more robust.

models.name: Combination: median of ETS, ARIMA, Theta
models.summary: Pointwise median of the automatic ETS, ARIMA and Theta forecasts.
models.how: The same three components as the mean combination; at each horizon step the middle value is taken, so a single badly wrong component has no effect. With one component failed it is the mean of the other two.
models.use: A robust alternative to the mean combination (the idea behind SCUM, with three components).
models.caution: As slow as its slowest component (ARIMA).

models.name: TBATS
models.summary: Exponential smoothing with trigonometric seasonality for series with multiple and fractional seasonal periods.
models.how: Box-Cox transformation, ARMA errors, trend and trigonometric (Fourier) seasonality; the components to use are selected by AIC. Periods may be fractional (e.g. 365.25).
models.use: When hourly/daily data have more than one seasonality.
models.caution: Very slow. NOT available in the Python engine: statsforecast AutoTBATS did not find the same model as R tbats() (disabled by user decision).

models.name: Auto ARIMA
models.summary: ARIMA with automatic selection of the differencing order and the (p,d,q)(P,D,Q) structure.
models.how: The differencing order is chosen by unit-root tests, and the orders by stepwise search and an information criterion; drift is allowed. Fallback chain: first with a log transformation (lambda=0), otherwise raw, otherwise non-seasonal.
models.use: A flexible classical method for series with strong autocorrelation.
models.caution: Slow; on long daily series (R) a single run can take about half an hour. The log transformation is tried only if all values are positive.

models.name: Dynamic harmonic regression (DHR-ARIMA)
models.summary: Models seasonality with Fourier terms and the remaining structure with a non-seasonal ARIMA.
models.how: For each seasonal period, K pairs of sin/cos terms are added as external regressors; the errors are modelled with auto.arima. K=1 in the original study.
models.use: Long or multi-seasonal periods (daily, weekly, hourly).
models.caution: As K grows the model is more flexible but slower and prone to overfitting.

models.name: Croston (classic)
models.summary: Smooths the demand size and the interval between demands separately; gives a flat forecast as a demand rate.
models.how: Only non-zero demands are exponentially smoothed; the interval between demands is smoothed separately. Forecast = size / interval, constant over the horizon.
models.use: Demand series with many zeros, such as spare parts.
models.caution: Produces a flat RATE (often below 1). If rounding to integers is on, it falls to 0: all forecasts can become 0. Turn rounding off. Classic Croston is known to be biased upwards.

models.name: Croston–SBA
models.summary: Applies to Croston the Syntetos–Boylan correction, which reduces its bias.
models.how: Shrinks the Croston forecast by a correction factor (approximately 1 − alpha/2).
models.use: To prevent Croston from consistently over-forecasting intermittent demand.
models.caution: Rounding to integers can turn forecasts into 0; turn rounding off.

models.name: Croston (optimised)
models.summary: Classic Croston; the smoothing parameter is optimised per series.
models.how: Instead of a fixed smoothing value, the parameter is chosen by the in-sample error.
models.use: When you do not want to choose the smoothing value by hand.
models.caution: On short and very sparse series the optimisation can be unstable. Turn rounding off.

models.name: TSB (Teunter–Syntetos–Babai)
models.summary: Updates the demand probability every period; for products whose demand stops, the forecast decays towards zero over time.
models.how: The demand probability (alpha_p) is smoothed every period, the demand size (alpha_d) only when demand occurs. Forecast = probability × size.
models.use: Products at risk of obsolescence: the Croston family does not update its forecast when demand stops.
models.caution: The default 0.1/0.1 is our own choice, not an evidence-based recommendation; tune it on your data. Turn rounding off.

models.name: ADIDA
models.summary: Reduces intermittency by temporal aggregation, forecasts, and then disaggregates the result.
models.how: The series is aggregated at one aggregation level (demand becomes less sparse), forecast with a simple method, and the forecast is divided back to the original scale.
models.use: An alternative to Croston on very sparse series.
models.caution: The aggregation level is chosen by the library. Turn rounding off.

models.name: IMAPA
models.summary: Combines the forecasts of several aggregation levels (MAPA for intermittent demand).
models.how: Forecasts are made at different aggregation levels and averaged; this reduces the risk of choosing a single level.
models.use: To avoid ADIDA's sensitivity to the choice of level.
models.caution: Turn rounding off.

models.name: Auto Theta
models.summary: Selects the best of the four Theta variants by in-sample error.
models.how: Standard, optimised, dynamic standard and dynamic optimised Theta models are tried; the library selects by its criterion.
models.use: An automated, more flexible version of Theta.
models.caution: For series containing zero/negative values, additive decomposition is used instead of multiplicative (a note is recorded). Without at least 2 periods of data the model is non-seasonal.

models.name: Complex exponential smoothing (CES)
models.summary: Smooths the series in the complex plane (real + imaginary component); selects the seasonality type automatically.
models.how: Captures trend and seasonality with complex-valued smoothing instead of separate components as in ETS.
models.use: Series with intertwined trend/seasonality where ETS falls short.
models.caution: If the period exceeds the 'largest seasonal period' setting the model is non-seasonal; this threshold (24) is our own choice.

models.name: Holt–Winters
models.summary: Tracks level, trend and seasonality with three separate exponential smoothings.
models.how: The classical three-component method; if there is no seasonality it reduces to Holt (a note is recorded).
models.use: Relatively short series with clear trend and seasonality.
models.caution: For multiplicative error all values must be greater than 0. The period threshold (24) is our own choice.

models.name: MSTL (multiple seasonal-trend decomposition)
models.summary: Decomposes the series into trend, several seasonal components and a remainder; trend/remainder are forecast with ETS.
models.how: STL decomposition is applied successively for each seasonal period. Periods are rounded to integers; only those with at least two periods of data are used.
models.use: Multiple seasonalities in hourly/daily data.
models.caution: If no valid period is found (e.g. yearly data) the series falls back to the fallback forecast; this is expected.

models.name: STL + ETS (stlf)
models.summary: R's stlf: STL removes the seasonality, ETS forecasts the seasonally adjusted series, the last seasonal cycle is added back.
models.how: Same as R forecast::stlf(y): mstl() with R's stl() settings (s.window 11, 15, … per period; one pass for one period, two passes for several; periods shorter than half the series), ets(model = "ZZN") on trend + remainder, the last cycle of each seasonal component repeated.
models.use: Seasonal daily/weekly data where a slowly changing seasonal pattern and a separate trend model are wanted; a strong, fast alternative to seasonal ETS (also for periods > 24, where ets() ignores seasonality).
models.caution: Needs a seasonal period and more than two full periods of data; otherwise the series falls back. Close to MSTL, which uses statsmodels' STL settings instead of R's.

models.name: STL + ARIMA
models.summary: As STL + ETS, but the seasonally adjusted series is forecast with a non-seasonal auto.arima.
models.how: R forecast(mstl(y), method = "arima"): the same R STL decomposition, auto.arima(seasonal = FALSE) on trend + remainder, the last seasonal cycle added back.
models.use: Seasonal series whose adjusted part has autocorrelation that ETS does not capture.
models.caution: Needs a seasonal period and more than two full periods of data; otherwise the series falls back.

models.name: Bagged ETS
models.summary: ETS fitted to the series and to bootstrapped copies of it; the forecasts are averaged.
models.how: R forecast::baggedETS after set.seed(seed): Box-Cox (Guerrero lambda in [0, 1] for positive data), periodic STL, a moving-block bootstrap of the remainder (blocks of two seasons) gives n_boot − 1 new series; ets() is fitted to each and to the original, and the point forecasts are averaged. R's random number generator is reproduced, so a seed gives R's numbers.
models.use: When ETS is a good model but its selection is unstable; bagging usually improves accuracy (strong on M3 monthly).
models.caution: About n_boot times the cost of ETS. Non-seasonal series (frequency 1, or fewer than two full periods) use R's loess trend instead of STL, as R does.

models.name: THieF (temporal hierarchies, ETS)
models.summary: Forecasts the series at every temporal aggregation level that divides the season (e.g. monthly, 2-monthly, quarterly, …, annual) and reconciles them.
models.how: R thief::thief(y, usemodel = "ets", comb = "struc"): non-overlapping sums at the levels that divide the seasonal period m, ets() at each level, then the forecasts are made coherent by structural-scaling weighted least squares; the reconciled bottom level is returned.
models.use: Monthly, quarterly or weekly data where the annual picture is more stable than the fine detail; typically improves on plain ETS.
models.caution: Needs a seasonal period m > 1 and at least two full periods of data; otherwise the series falls back. Levels with very short series use R's small-sample ETS branch.

models.name: MAPA (multiple aggregation prediction)
models.summary: ETS at temporal aggregation levels 1..m; the level, trend and seasonal components are combined across levels.
models.how: R MAPA::mapa(y, comb = "w.mean", hybrid = TRUE, model = "ZZZ", type = "ets"): the series is averaged over 1..m periods, ets() is fitted at each level, the final states are translated into level / trend / season forecasts, level and trend are averaged, the seasonal parts of the levels that divide m are combined with 1/AL weights, and the result is averaged with the level-1 ETS forecast.
models.use: Noisy series where the model chosen at the original frequency is unstable; strong on intermittent and monthly data.
models.caution: About m ETS fits per series. Aggregation levels with fewer than four observations are skipped, as in R.

models.name: Auto MFLES
models.summary: Gradient-boosted time-series decomposition: trend, seasonal and level steps are learned in sequence.
models.how: The library selects its settings by taking the last 'horizon' observations as test windows (n_windows of them); the criterion can be chosen.
models.use: To try a quick modern alternative to classical methods.
models.caution: Requires scikit-learn. A peer-reviewed reference has not been verified; cite the library documentation before using it in a paper.

models.name: Holt (ETS with additive trend)
models.summary: Exponential smoothing of level and trend, with the trend damped or not as the information criterion decides.
models.how: ETS(A,A,N) and ETS(A,Ad,N) (or the multiplicative-error forms) are fitted and the one with the lower AICc is kept.
models.use: Trended, non-seasonal series; a classical benchmark between SES and the full automatic ETS.
models.caution: For multiplicative error all values must be greater than 0. Seasonality is ignored; use ETS or Holt-Winters for seasonal data.

models.name: Historic average
models.summary: Forecasts every future value with the mean of the whole training series.
models.how: The arithmetic mean of all observations is repeated over the horizon (R: meanf).
models.use: The simplest benchmark for stationary series without trend or seasonality.
models.caution: Ignores trend, seasonality and recent level shifts; only useful as a lower bound.

models.name: Window average
models.summary: Forecasts with the mean of the last few observations.
models.how: The mean of the last window_size values is repeated over the horizon.
models.use: A benchmark that follows level shifts more quickly than the historic average.
models.caution: A series shorter than the window falls back. The default window (4) is our own choice.

models.name: Seasonal window average
models.summary: Forecasts each season position with the mean of that position over the last few seasons.
models.how: The last window_size full seasons are averaged position by position and the seasonal profile is repeated.
models.use: A seasonal benchmark that is less noisy than the seasonal naive method (daily data with weekly cycles, NN5).
models.caution: Needs window_size full seasons, otherwise the series falls back; without a usable season it is the window average.

models.name: Seasonal exponential smoothing (optimised)
models.summary: Simple exponential smoothing run separately on each season position, with its own optimised alpha.
models.how: The series is split into its m season positions; SES with alpha chosen in [0.01, 0.99] by golden-section search forecasts each one.
models.use: Seasonal series whose seasonal pattern changes slowly; a smoother alternative to the seasonal naive method.
models.caution: There is no trend component. A series shorter than one season falls back.

models.name: Zero forecast
models.summary: Forecasts zero for every period.
models.how: Returns 0 over the whole horizon.
models.use: Sanity baseline for intermittent demand (M5): a model that cannot beat it on a given metric adds nothing.
models.caution: Only meaningful for intermittent series and for metrics that do not divide by the forecast; rounding has no effect on it.

models.name: Standard Theta model (STM)
models.summary: The Theta method written as a state-space model, with the theta coefficient fixed at 2.
models.how: The model of Fiorucci et al. (2016): a smoothed level plus (1 − 1/θ) times a linear trend fitted once to the whole series, θ = 2; the starting level and the smoothing parameter are chosen by minimising the in-sample squared error. Seasonality is removed first by classical decomposition when an autocorrelation test detects it.
models.use: The state-space counterpart of the classical Theta method; the reference point for the optimised and dynamic variants.
models.caution: For series containing zero/negative values, additive decomposition is used instead of multiplicative (a note is recorded). Without at least 2 periods of data the model is non-seasonal. Not the same code as the method 'theta' (R thetaf), so the two differ slightly.

models.name: Optimised Theta model (OTM)
models.summary: The standard Theta model with the theta coefficient estimated from the data instead of fixed at 2.
models.how: As the standard Theta model, but θ ≥ 1 is optimised together with the starting level and the smoothing parameter (in-sample squared error). θ = 1 gives simple exponential smoothing, larger values give more weight to the long-run trend.
models.use: Series whose trend is weaker or stronger than the fixed θ = 2 assumes; in M3 it improved on the standard Theta method.
models.caution: For series containing zero/negative values, additive decomposition is used instead of multiplicative (a note is recorded). Without at least 2 periods of data the model is non-seasonal. One more parameter to estimate, so short series can overfit.

models.name: Dynamic standard Theta model (DSTM)
models.summary: The standard Theta model (θ = 2) with a trend line that is re-estimated at every time point.
models.how: As the standard Theta model, but the intercept and slope of the linear trend are updated recursively as each observation arrives, instead of being fitted once to the whole series.
models.use: Series whose trend changes over time; the fixed-θ companion of DOTM.
models.caution: For series containing zero/negative values, additive decomposition is used instead of multiplicative (a note is recorded). Without at least 2 periods of data the model is non-seasonal.

models.name: BATS (non-seasonal)
models.summary: Exponential smoothing in state-space form with an optional Box-Cox transformation, ARMA errors, trend and damping.
models.how: The model TBATS compares its seasonal candidates with (R: bats() on the series without a seasonal period): with and without Box-Cox transformation, trend and damped trend, each also with ARMA errors chosen by auto.arima on the residuals; the combination with the lowest AIC is kept.
models.use: Trended series without seasonality whose variance grows with the level, or whose errors are autocorrelated; also shows what the seasonal part of TBATS adds on your data.
models.caution: Seasonality is ignored: the seasonal BATS model is not offered here, use TBATS for seasonal data. Box-Cox is tried only when all values are positive. Slower than ETS (up to twelve fits per series).

models.name: Structural time series (StructTS)
models.summary: A level, a slope and a seasonal component that each change randomly over time, estimated with the Kalman filter.
models.how: The basic structural model of Harvey (1989): local level, local slope and a dummy-variable seasonal, each with its own disturbance variance plus observation noise; the variances are found by maximum likelihood (R: StructTS, optim L-BFGS-B). The seasonal component is used when the period is at most 24 and the series holds two full periods; otherwise the local linear trend model is fitted. It has no settings.
models.use: An interpretable alternative to ETS and ARIMA whose components can be read directly; handles slowly changing trend and seasonality.
models.caution: The likelihood is flat for many series, so the optimiser can stop at a boundary (a variance of 0) or at a local optimum. Cost grows with the cube of the period, which is why longer periods are fitted without a seasonal part.

models.name: Double seasonal Holt-Winters (DSHW)
models.summary: Holt-Winters exponential smoothing with two multiplicative seasonal cycles, one nested in the other.
models.how: Taylor's (2003) method: a level, a trend and two sets of multiplicative seasonal indices (for example the day within half-hourly data and the week), plus a first-order autoregressive correction of the errors. The five parameters minimise the in-sample squared error (R: dshw). With more than two periods the two shortest are used.
models.use: Half-hourly or hourly series with a daily and a weekly cycle (electricity demand, call volumes), for short horizons.
models.caution: Needs two seasonal periods where the longer is a whole multiple of the shorter (48 and 336, 24 and 168), strictly positive data and at least two of the longer periods; any other series falls back. Data with one period (monthly, NN5 daily) cannot use it.

models.name: Neural network autoregression (NNAR)
models.summary: A small feed-forward neural network per series that predicts the next value from its own lagged values.
models.how: R nnetar(): the series is standardised; the inputs are the last p values (p chosen by an autoregression's AIC, on the seasonally adjusted series when there is a season) and the value one season back; one hidden layer of round((inputs + 1) / 2) logistic units and a linear output are fitted by least squares (BFGS, at most 100 iterations). 'repeats' networks from different random starting weights are averaged, and forecasts are fed back as inputs for the next step.
models.use: Series with non-linear dynamics that linear models miss; a classical neural benchmark that needs no other series.
models.caution: The networks often stop at the iteration limit and depend on the random starting weights, so the seed changes the forecast; results are reproducible for a given seed. No differencing is applied, so strongly trended series are extrapolated poorly. Short series give few training rows for many weights (overfitting).

models.name: Linear trend with seasonal dummies (TSLM)
models.summary: An ordinary least-squares regression of the series on a straight time trend and one dummy variable per season.
models.how: y(t) = a + b·t + s(season of t) is fitted by least squares (R: tslm(y ~ trend + season)); the forecast extends the line and repeats the seasonal effects. Seasonal dummies are used when the period is at most 366 and the series holds two full periods; otherwise only the trend is fitted. It has no settings.
models.use: A transparent benchmark for series with a steady trend and a fixed seasonal pattern; every coefficient has a direct reading.
models.caution: The trend is one global straight line and the seasonal pattern never changes, so a level shift or a bend in the trend is extrapolated wrongly; errors grow with the horizon. A long period uses one coefficient per season (52 for weekly data), which overfits short series.

metrics.name: SMAPE
metrics.text: Mean of 2·|forecast−actual| / (|forecast|+|actual|). Given as a ratio (0–2), NOT a percentage. It is undefined when forecast and actual are both 0, and that point is excluded.
metrics.caution: Misleading for intermittent demand: every point with forecast 0 and actual > 0 gives exactly 2; a model that forecasts all zeros scores exactly 2.0.

metrics.name: mSMAPE
metrics.text: A form of SMAPE corrected (epsilon = 0.1) so that its denominator does not blow up for small values.
metrics.caution: Reduces SMAPE's zero problem but does not remove it.

metrics.name: MASE
metrics.text: Mean absolute error / mean absolute error of the seasonal naive on the training part (lag = seasonal period). Below 1 means better than seasonal naive.
metrics.caution: If the whole training part is zero the denominator is 0 (the series is excluded). With intermittent demand it can reward zero forecasts.

metrics.name: MAE
metrics.caution: With intermittent demand it rewards the median (often 0) forecast; it can be meaningless for inventory.

metrics.name: RMSE
metrics.text: Square root of the mean of squared errors; penalises large errors more.
metrics.caution: Computed per series and then averaged across series; watch the scale effect when comparing series of different scales.

metrics.name: WAPE
metrics.caution: Undefined if the total of actuals is 0. A model that forecasts all zeros scores exactly 100%.

metrics.name: nRMSE (range)
metrics.text: RMSE / (maximum of actuals − minimum of actuals).

metrics.name: RMSSE
metrics.text: Root of: mean squared error / mean squared one-step naive error on the training part (the M5 measure). Below 1 means better than the in-sample naive.
metrics.caution: The scale uses the whole training part; the official M5 definition starts at the first non-zero sale, which differs only for series with leading zeros.

metrics.name: MSE
metrics.caution: Scale-dependent; do not average across series of different scales.

metrics.name: MAPE
metrics.caution: Points with actual = 0 are excluded; asymmetric (penalises over-forecasts more). Not suitable for intermittent demand.

metrics.name: MAAPE
metrics.text: Mean of arctan(|error| / |actual|); bounded, defined when the actual is 0.
metrics.caution: A zero forecast for a positive actual scores about 0.785 (π/4) per point, so it can still favour zero forecasts on intermittent data.

metrics.name: MedAE
metrics.text: Median absolute error over the horizon.
metrics.caution: Robust to a few large errors; scale-dependent.

metrics.name: RMSLE
metrics.text: Root mean squared difference of log(1 + forecast) and log(1 + actual).
metrics.caution: Undefined (series excluded) if any forecast or actual is negative; no clipping is applied.

metrics.name: ME (bias)
metrics.text: Mean of forecast − actual. Positive: over-forecasting.
metrics.caution: Positive and negative errors cancel; read together with an absolute measure.

metrics.name: Percent bias
metrics.caution: Undefined if the actuals sum to 0. Shows when a 'winning' model is simply biased toward zero.

basic.text: Number of observations (missing values not counted).
Standard deviation of the series (divisor n − 1).
Coefficient of variation: standard deviation divided by the absolute mean. Undefined when the mean is 0.
Share of observations that are exactly 0.
Average demand interval: number of observations divided by the number of non-zero observations. 1 means demand in every period; larger values mean rarer demand.
Squared coefficient of variation of the non-zero values: how much the size of the demand varies when there is demand.
Box-Cox transformation parameter chosen by Guerrero's method between −1 and 2 (as forecast::BoxCox.lambda in R): near 1 the series needs no transformation, near 0 a logarithm stabilises its variance.

classes.text: Demand in most periods, sizes that vary little (ADI below 1.32, CV² below 0.49).
Demand in few periods, sizes that vary little (ADI 1.32 or more, CV² below 0.49).
Demand in most periods, sizes that vary a lot (ADI below 1.32, CV² 0.49 or more).
Demand in few periods, sizes that vary a lot (ADI 1.32 or more, CV² 0.49 or more).

catch22.text: 5-bin histogram mode.
10-bin histogram mode.
First 1/e crossing of the autocorrelation function.
First minimum of the autocorrelation function.
Histogram-based automutual information (lag 2, 5 bins).
Time reversibility.
Proportion of high incremental changes in the series.
Longest stretch of above-mean values.
Transition matrix column variance (series coarse-grained to three symbols).
Wang's periodicity metric.
Goodness of exponential fit to the embedding distance distribution.
First minimum of the automutual information function.
Change in autocorrelation timescale after incremental differencing.
Positive outlier timing.
Negative outlier timing.
Power in the lowest 20% of frequencies.
Longest stretch of non-increasing values.
Entropy of successive pairs in the symbolized series.
Rescaled range fluctuation analysis (low-scale scaling).
Detrended fluctuation analysis (low-scale scaling).
Centroid frequency of the power spectrum (the frequency that splits its power in half).
Error of a 3-point rolling mean forecast.

tsfeatures.text: Mean of the series (shown as tsf_mean next to the descriptive mean; the two are equal).
Variance of the series (divisor n − 1). All the following characteristics are computed on the series scaled to mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

Largest change in the distribution of the values between two consecutive windows (Kullback-Leibler divergence of kernel density estimates), and where in the series it occurs. The window is one seasonal period long, or 10 observations for non-seasonal data.
Largest change in the mean between two consecutive windows, and where it occurs.
Largest change in the variance between two consecutive windows, and where it occurs.
First autocorrelation of the series, and the sum of squares of its first ten autocorrelations.
The same two numbers for the differenced and the twice-differenced series.
Autocorrelation at the first seasonal lag (seasonal data only).

R² of a regression of the squared, mean-corrected series on its 12 previous values: how far the size of the fluctuations depends on recent ones (Engle's test statistic for ARCH effects). For a series whose last values are all equal the regression fits exactly and the value carries no information.
Number of times the series crosses its median.
Spectral entropy (0 to 1): close to 0 for a series dominated by trend or seasonality, close to 1 for one that resembles noise. A measure of how forecastable the series is.
Longest run of consecutive observations in the same tenth of the range of the series.
Smoothing parameters of Holt's linear trend method fitted to the series (level and trend).
Hurst exponent, from the fractional differencing order of a fitted long-memory model (d + 0.5): above 0.5 for a series with long memory.
Variance of the variances of consecutive, non-overlapping windows: how unevenly the variability is spread.
Variance of the means of the same windows: how much the level moves.
Statistic of Teräsvirta's neural-network test for nonlinearity, scaled; large for series that a linear autoregression describes poorly.
Sum of squares of the first five partial autocorrelations of the series, of the differenced and of the twice-differenced series.
Partial autocorrelation at the first seasonal lag (seasonal data only).
KPSS statistic for the hypothesis that the series is stationary around a level; large values point to a unit root.
Phillips-Perron statistic for the hypothesis of a unit root; strongly negative values point to stationarity.
Number of seasonal periods of the data and their lengths (the same for every series of a file).
Strength of the trend (0 to 1) in an STL decomposition: 1 − variance of the remainder / variance of the deseasonalised series.
Strength of the seasonality (0 to 1) in the same decomposition: 1 − variance of the remainder / variance of the detrended series (seasonal data only).
Variance of the leave-one-out variances of the remainder: large when a few observations are far from the rest.
Coefficients of the linear and the quadratic term when an orthogonal quadratic is fitted to the trend component.
First autocorrelation of the remainder, and the sum of squares of its first ten autocorrelations.
Position within the seasonal cycle of the largest and of the smallest seasonal effect (seasonal data only).

map: The map is a principal component analysis (PCA) of the characteristics. Each characteristic is first standardised (mean 0, standard deviation 1), so that none dominates because of its unit; this is a PCA on the correlation matrix. A characteristic that is constant, or missing for more than half of the series, is left out; other missing values are replaced by the median.

The first component (PC1) is the direction along which the series differ most, PC2 the next one that is unrelated to it, and so on. The percentage next to each axis is the share of the total variation it shows; when PC1 and PC2 together show a small share, the flat picture hides much of the difference between series.

Each point is one series. Two points close together are series with similar characteristics; the distance to the centre says how unusual a series is. The arrows (loadings) show which characteristics pull the points in which direction: a series far along an arrow has a high value of that characteristic. The sign of a component has no meaning of its own.

Colouring the map by the error of a run shows where on the map a method does well or badly, that is, for which kind of series. This is the idea of the instance space of Kang, Hyndman and Smith-Miles (2017).
